newsitem.title: UK: UK minutes show George urged immediate rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK minutes show George urged immediate rate rise.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George told then Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on April 10 that he should make a start on tightening UK monetary policy by raising interest rates immediately by a quarter-point, minutes of their meeting published on Wednesday showed.

"The need for a tightening of monetary policy, if we were to stand any reasonable chance of meeting the inflation target two years ahead had....become more urgent, and the Bank continued to recommend making a start now by raising interest rates by a quarter percent," the minutes quoted George as saying.
New Chancellor Gordon Brown raised interest rates by a quarter-point earlier this month just five days after his Labour Party's landslide election victory.
But the minutes showed Clarke resisted a rate rise, telling George it would be seen by markets as the first in a series.

"The Chancellor said that he and the Governor were only a quarter percentage point apart on interest rates. But he was concerned that even a small rise in interest rates might be viewed by the market as the first in a series of interest rate increases. This could cause the pound to rise further," the minutes said.
Clarke said the appreciation of the pound "would have a similar affect on activity and inflation to a rise in interest rates."
The minutes showed that George had been concerned by recent monetary data and figures on domestic demand and output which had been uniformly strong.
"That reinforced the Bank's concern that the inflation target was now at significant risk, looking two years ahead," they said.

"The Governor said there was no doubt that sterling's appreciation was having a dampening effect on costs and prices in the short-term, but perhaps less of an effect, so far at least, than might have been expected," the minutes said.
Clarke's Conservative government had a 2.5 percent target for underlying inflation, one that Brown has adopted. That target was finally met in April, official data out last week showed.

The minutes showed that despite the relatively limited effects of the appreciation of sterling on prices, "the Bank continued to assume that the appreciation would reduce the rate of retail price inflation to below 2.5 percent in the course of this year and that it would lead to a weakening of net external demand," the minutes said.
